title: Threats: brute force, DoS, interception, SQL injection
specPoints: Forms of attack: **brute-force attacks**, **denial of service (DoS)** attacks, **data interception and theft**
Outline the **impact** of each attack on an organisation
learn: Describe how a brute-force attack works and calculate why longer passwords defeat it
Describe a denial of service attack and its effect on an organisation
Explain how data can be intercepted on a network (packet sniffing, man-in-the-middle) and why encryption protects it
Explain the concept of SQL injection with a simple example of what the attacker types and what happens
Match each attack to a specific impact on a business, school or hospital
hook: Write a 4-digit PIN on a sticky note and keep it secret. I will guess it. 0000, 0001, 0002... How long until I get there? There are only 10,000 PINs; a computer tries them in under a second. Now make it 8 characters with letters, numbers and symbols. The same computer needs years. Today's attacks are about speed, flooding, listening in, and typing something a website did not expect.

video.title: Four technical attacks in four minutes
video.brief: 4 minutes, one scene per attack. Brute force: a padlock with a counter spinning through combinations; the counter for 4 digits stops fast, the 8-character one keeps spinning as the screen fades. DoS: a shop door with one customer, then a thousand fake customers blocking it so real ones cannot get in. Interception: two people passing a postcard across a room while a third reads it; then the postcard is replaced by a sealed envelope (encryption) and the reader sees nothing. SQL injection: a login box; a user types a name, then an attacker types a quote mark and OR 1=1 and the database says yes to everyone. Close: each attack has a matching defence, which is next lesson.

p: A **brute-force attack** tries every possible password or key until one works. It is not clever: it is fast. Software can try thousands of guesses per second against a weak system. A smarter version, a **dictionary attack**, tries common words and leaked passwords first.
The defence is maths. The number of possible passwords is **(number of symbols) to the power of (length)**. Doubling the length squares the work.
explain.code:
Password type                  Possibilities        Time at 1,000 guesses/second
-----------------------------  -------------------  ----------------------------
4-digit PIN (0-9)              10^4 = 10,000        10 seconds
6 lowercase letters (a-z)      26^6 = 308,915,776   about 3.6 days
8 chars, upper+lower+digits    62^8 = 2.18 x 10^14  about 6,900 years
12 chars, 95 printable symbols 95^12 = 5.4 x 10^23  longer than the age of the universe
after: Impact on an organisation: a cracked password gives the attacker **the same access as the user**, so the damage depends on what that user can do. That is why access levels matter.

p: A **denial of service attack** floods a server with so many requests that it cannot respond to genuine users. The website slows or crashes. A **DDoS** (distributed DoS) uses many infected computers (a **botnet**) to send the flood at once, which makes it hard to block by IP address.
Nothing is stolen. The impact is **downtime**: an online shop loses sales for every minute it is offline; a school cannot access its cloud systems; customers lose trust and go elsewhere.

Data moving across a network travels in **packets**. If the network is unencrypted (public Wi-Fi, an old protocol such as HTTP), an attacker on the same network can capture those packets with a **packet sniffer** and read them: usernames, passwords, card details, messages.

A **man-in-the-middle attack** goes further: the attacker sits between the user and the server, relaying traffic so both sides think they are talking directly, while reading or changing everything that passes.
The defence is **encryption**: the attacker still captures the packets but sees only scrambled ciphertext without the key.

Many websites store users in a database and check logins with an **SQL query**. If the site builds that query by **gluing the user's typing straight into the SQL**, the user can type SQL of their own, and the database will run it. This is **SQL injection**.
Suppose the site builds this query from the username box:
explain.code:
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + typed + "' AND password = '" + pwd + "'"

Normal user types:    alice
Query becomes:        ... WHERE username = 'alice' AND password = 'xyz'

Attacker types:       ' OR '1'='1
Query becomes:        ... WHERE username = '' OR '1'='1' AND password = ''

'1'='1' is always TRUE, so the WHERE clause matches rows
without knowing any password -> the attacker is logged in.
Worse: a typed  '; DROP TABLE users; --  could delete the table.
after: Impact: the attacker can **read**, **change** or **delete** data in the database — customer records, grades, prices. For the exam you need the **concept**: user input is treated as code. The fix (next lesson) is **input validation** and **parameterised queries**, where the database treats typing as plain text, never as SQL.

p: Exam questions reward impacts that fit the attack. Use this table when a scenario asks 'explain the impact'.
explain.code:
Attack              What the attacker gets          Typical impact on organisation
------------------  ------------------------------  -------------------------------------
Brute force         A valid account/password        Unauthorised access; data theft
DoS / DDoS          Nothing - just disruption       Downtime; lost sales; lost trust
Interception        Copies of data in transit       Stolen passwords/card details; fines
SQL injection       Read/change/delete database     Data breach; corrupted records; fines

p: The attacker tries every password, one after another, very fast. A short password is found quickly. A long one with many symbol types takes years.
simple.code:
4-digit PIN:   10,000 guesses   -> seconds
8 mixed chars: 218 trillion     -> thousands of years

p: The attacker sends millions of fake requests to a website. It gets so busy that real people cannot get in. Nothing is stolen, but the site is down and the business loses money.
Data travels across networks in packets. On an unprotected network, an attacker can capture and read them. This is packet sniffing. Encryption scrambles the data so a captured packet is useless.

A website asks for your username. It puts your typing straight into a database command. An attacker types database code instead of a name. The database runs it. The attacker can log in without a password, or delete data.
simple.code:
Attacker types:  ' OR '1'='1
This is always true, so the login says yes.

keyterms.def: Trying every possible password or key, usually automatically, until the correct one is found.
Flooding a server with requests so that it cannot serve genuine users.
A DoS attack launched from many compromised computers (a botnet) at once.
Capturing data as it travels across a network, for example with a packet sniffer.
An attack where the attacker secretly relays, reads or alters traffic between two parties who believe they are communicating directly.
Entering SQL code into an input box so that a badly written website runs it against its database.
Software that captures and inspects packets travelling on a network.

try.title: 1. Brute force by numbers
p: This program does **not** crack anything. It counts how many guesses a brute-force attack would need and how long that takes. Run it, then change the guesses-per-second to 1,000,000,000 (a modern cracking rig) and see which passwords survive.
try.code:
# How long would brute force take? (maths only - nothing is attacked)
guesses_per_second = 1000

password_types = [
    ("4-digit PIN",              10, 4),
    ("6 lowercase letters",      26, 6),
    ("8 letters + digits",       62, 8),
    ("12 chars, any symbol",     95, 12),
]

def nice_time(seconds):
    units = [("years", 31536000), ("days", 86400), ("hours", 3600), ("minutes", 60), ("seconds", 1)]
    for name, size in units:
        if seconds >= size:
            return str(round(seconds / size, 1)) + " " + name
    return "under a second"

for name, symbols, length in password_types:
    possibilities = symbols ** length
    seconds = possibilities / guesses_per_second
    print(name.ljust(24), "{:,}".format(possibilities).rjust(28), "->", nice_time(seconds))

# TODO 1: set guesses_per_second = 1000000000 and rerun.
# TODO 2: add your own row: how many symbols and how long is YOUR password style?

try.title: 2. Interception: plaintext vs ciphertext
p: Two devices send a message across a network while a third copies every packet. Run it: the sniffer reads the first message easily. Then look at the second, which has been scrambled with a toy XOR cipher before sending. The attacker captured the same number of bytes but cannot read them without the key.
try.code:
# Toy demonstration of why encryption defeats interception.
# XOR with a one-byte key is NOT real security - it just shows the idea.

def xor_encrypt(text, key):
    return [ord(ch) ^ key for ch in text]

def xor_decrypt(numbers, key):
    return "".join(chr(n ^ key) for n in numbers)

message = "card 4921 pin 3310"

# --- Message 1: sent in plaintext (like HTTP on open Wi-Fi) ---
packet1 = message
print("Sniffer captures packet 1:", packet1)

# --- Message 2: encrypted before sending (like HTTPS) ---
key = 42
packet2 = xor_encrypt(message, key)
print("Sniffer captures packet 2:", packet2)
print("Sniffer tries to read it:  ", "".join(chr(n) for n in packet2))

# Only the receiver has the key
print("Receiver decrypts:          ", xor_decrypt(packet2, key))

# TODO: change the key to 7. Does the sniffer's view change? Does the receiver still read it?
# Extension: why would a one-byte key still be weak against brute force? (Hint: how many keys?)

try.title: 3. SQL injection: glued string vs placeholder
p: No real database here: a tiny fake 'database' checks a login two ways. Way A glues the typing into the query (vulnerable). Way B treats typing as plain data (safe). Run it with a normal username and then with the injection string, and compare the results.
try.code:
# Conceptual demo - a pretend database that can only do one thing.
# It shows WHY building queries from user typing is dangerous.

users = {"alice": "s3cret", "bob": "hunter2"}

def fake_db_run(query_text):
    # Our toy 'database' understands exactly one trick: a literal OR '1'='1 is always true.
    if "OR '1'='1'" in query_text:
        return True          # the WHERE clause matched every row
    # otherwise pull the two quoted values back out and check them properly
    parts = query_text.split("'")
    name, pwd = parts[1], parts[3]
    return users.get(name) == pwd

def login_glued(name, pwd):            # WAY A - vulnerable
    query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + name + "' AND password = '" + pwd + "'"
    print("  query sent:", query)
    return fake_db_run(query)

def login_parameterised(name, pwd):    # WAY B - safe
    # The typing is NEVER joined into the query text. It is checked as data only.
    print("  query sent: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?   params:", (name, pwd))
    return users.get(name) == pwd

attempts = [("alice", "s3cret"), ("alice", "wrong"), ("' OR '1'='1", "anything")]

for name, pwd in attempts:
    print("Typed username:", repr(name))
    print("  glued ->         ", "LOGGED IN" if login_glued(name, pwd) else "refused")
    print("  parameterised -> ", "LOGGED IN" if login_parameterised(name, pwd) else "refused")
    print()

# Question: in which version does the attacker's typing become part of the command?

Pick one and write a two-sentence impact for a hospital. First sentence: what happens. Second: what that means for patients.

exam.q: Describe how a **brute-force attack** is carried out.
model: Software repeatedly tries different passwords/keys (1), working through every possible combination (or a list of common passwords) until the correct one is found (1).
exam.commentary: 'Guessing the password' alone is one mark. The second mark is for *systematically trying all combinations* or *automated/many attempts*. Mentioning a dictionary of common passwords is creditable.

exam.q: A ticket website crashes on the morning tickets go on sale. The company suspects a DDoS attack. Explain how a DDoS attack causes a website to become unavailable.
model: Many computers (a botnet of infected machines) send requests to the server at the same time (1). The server cannot handle the volume of traffic / runs out of bandwidth or processing capacity (1), so genuine users' requests time out or are refused (1).
exam.commentary: Three ideas: many sources, server overwhelmed, real users locked out. Students often forget the third — the *denial* to genuine users is the point of the name. Confusing this with heavy legitimate demand loses the first mark.

exam.q: A website checks logins by building the SQL query `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '[typed name]'` directly from the text a user types. Explain how an attacker could use **SQL injection** on this site, and state **one** impact on the website's owner.
model: The attacker types SQL code into the name box instead of a name (1), e.g. `' OR '1'='1` (1). Because the typing is joined into the query, the database runs the attacker's code, so the condition is always true / extra commands run and the attacker is logged in or can read, change or delete data (1). Impact: customer data stolen / records deleted or altered / fine and reputational damage (1).
exam.commentary: The concept mark is *input is treated as code*. An example string helps but is not essential; a clear statement that the typed text becomes part of the query earns the mark. 'Hacking the database' with no mechanism scores zero for the explain part.

home: Using the brute-force table, work out how many possibilities there are for (a) a 6-digit PIN, (b) a 10-character password using lowercase letters only, (c) a 10-character password using 95 symbols. Then write two sentences explaining to a friend why 'longer' beats 'more complicated'.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 5 · explain 15 · try 25 · check 5 · exam 8 · homework 2
misconceptions: DoS 'steals data'. It does not: it denies access. Impact words are downtime, lost sales, lost trust.
Brute force 'hacks the password'. Be precise: it guesses systematically; it is beaten by length, lockouts and two-factor.
SQL injection explained as 'typing a virus'. It is typing SQL that the site mistakenly runs. The key phrase: input treated as code.
Encryption 'stops interception'. It does not stop the capture; it makes the captured data unreadable.
say: 'Brute force is not clever. It is fast. Make it slow with length.'
'A DoS attack is a thousand fake customers in the doorway.'
'If your typing can become part of the command, you own the database.'
teacher.skip: Try 2 can go if time is short; Try 1 and Try 3 carry the two calculation/concept ideas the exam asks about. Try 5 is a quick plenary.
differentiation: Support: in Try 3, just run it and highlight the one line where the typed text appears inside the query. That is the whole idea.
Stretch: in Try 2, write a loop that brute-forces the one-byte XOR key (only 256 to try) and explain why real keys are 128 bits or more.
